strengths: BiAlign addresses a relevant NLP problem: transferring in-context learning capabilities to smaller models. Matching teacher and student preferences over demonstration subsets is a plausible extension to output distillation and requires no additional inference-time machinery.

The evaluation covers five benchmark families with stated separation between training and evaluation tasks. Table 2 reports improvements across all five benchmarks, with average performance increasing from 29.2 for Output-Align to 30.2 for BiAlign.

The main approach is clearly illustrated and accompanied by equations and pseudocode. Comparisons with fine-tuning, continual pretraining, and output alignment are useful, as are the sensitivity analyses concerning subset counts and demonstration counts.
weaknesses: The experiments do not adequately isolate the central contribution. Compared with Output-Align, BiAlign adds both teacher-guided ranking and training on additional demonstration subsets. A baseline applying ordinary distillation to the same sampled subsets, with comparable training resources, is needed to distinguish the benefit of preference alignment from additional context variation. Measuring teacher–student ranking agreement would also substantiate the proposed mechanism.

The reliability of the improvements is insufficiently established. No run counts, variability estimates, or significance analyses are reported despite stochastic training and demonstration sampling. Several gains over competing baselines are small: 0.2 percentage points over Output-Align on MMLU and 0.3 over continual pretraining on GSM8K. The HumanEval improvement over Vanilla corresponds to approximately one additional solved problem. These results are encouraging but do not yet establish robust superiority or preservation of zero-shot capabilities.

The HumanEval reporting needs reconciliation. Under the stated greedy evaluation on 164 problems, the FT score of 14.2% and C-Pretrain score of 13.2% cannot arise from a single binary pass/fail evaluation, even after rounding to one decimal place. If these are averages across runs or use another aggregation protocol, that protocol and its variability must be specified.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Although several hyperparameters are provided, the manuscript does not adequately specify the exact CrossFit construction, optimizer and schedule, sequence truncation, or evaluation prompts and answer extraction. No implementation or configuration link is supplied, and the appendix is empty. Equation 3 also needs explicit handling of tied rankings and a zero student-score range. These omissions matter when reproducing comparatively small performance differences.

The broader claims exceed the demonstrated scope. Experiments use only one teacher–student pair, Llama 2-13B and 7B; the source-task diversity analysis does not establish that training-data volume is controlled; and additional training costs are unreported. The reasoning explanation rests largely on one qualitative example. These limitations constrain the broader contribution, while the missing controls, uncertainty estimates, and reproducibility details are the decisive reasons for recommending revision next cycle.
